:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The chain rule can be used to differentiate logarithmic functions like 

$$
y = \ln (2x+1).
$$

First notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \ln u, \qquad u = 2x+1.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x+1,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = \ln u, \qquad u = x^2-4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = 2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$
